meta.title: Shirakawa Park Nagoya: Science Museum, Art Museum & Parking Guide
meta.description: A complete visitor guide to Shirakawa Park in Sakae, Nagoya: highlights of the Nagoya City Science Museum (world's largest planetarium) and Nagoya City Art Museum, cherry blossom season, nearby parking and typical rates, access from Fushimi Station, and 24-hour free admission.

hero.title: Shirakawa Park
hero.subtitle: Where art, science and greenery intertwine — a cultural gravity point in central Nagoya. A 'green lung' reborn after the war, crowned to the north by the world's largest planetarium dome and embraced to the south by a temple of art. Cherry blossoms in spring, golden ginkgo in autumn, open 24 hours — a hidden natural sanctuary beside the bustling Sakae district.

intro.title: Discover Shirakawa Park
intro.description: Shirakawa Park is one of central Nagoya's most beloved green spaces, lying in the Sakae district of Naka Ward between the Nagoya City Science Museum and the Nagoya City Art Museum. Opened in 1931, it is a classic urban park of lawns, tree-lined paths and seasonal flower beds. Every spring roughly 120 cherry trees turn the grounds pink, while in autumn the ginkgo and maple leaves colour the avenues. With no admission fee and 24-hour access, it is a calm retreat for locals, families and visitors exploring the museums that flank it.

visitGuide.title: Visitor Guide
visitGuide.description: As a public park open 24 hours, Shirakawa Park can be visited at any time; early morning and weekday afternoons are the quietest.
items: Plan 30 minutes to an hour: stroll the lawns, photograph the cherry blossoms (late March–early April) or the autumn leaves.
The park sits between the Nagoya City Science Museum (north) and the Nagoya City Art Museum (south) — combine all three in one visit.
Paths are flat and paved, but shade is limited in summer: bring water, a hat and sunscreen.
It is a short walk from Sakae and Fushimi, the two main hubs of central Nagoya.

transportSection.subtitle: We'll breeze through long-distance travel and focus on the 'last mile': the park is an easy walk from the nearest subway stations.
transportSection.overviewText: Nagoya is reached by the Tokaido Shinkansen, by air via Chubu Centrair International Airport (NGO), or by highway bus. Once in the city, Shirakawa Park lies in Naka Ward near Sakae; the nearest subway stations are Fushimi and Sakae, each only a 5–10 minute walk away.
transportSection.arrivalTitle: Know this before you set out
arrivalItems: The park is in central Nagoya, Naka Ward, 2-17 Sakae — flat and easy to reach on foot from Sakae or Fushimi.
The park has no dedicated parking; use the municipal underground car parks nearby.
Cherry season and weekends get crowded; go early in the morning to beat the crowds.

parking.title: Parking Guide
parking.summary: There is no visitor car park inside the park; use the time-based car parks nearby.
items: Several private time-based car parks are distributed around the park (toward Sakae and Fushimi), typically billed per 30 minutes and often with a daily maximum (cap) rate.
Rates and caps vary by lot and time of day — please check the on-site price board before entering.
Weekday daytime is usually easier; weekend, public-holiday and cherry-season mornings fill up quickly.
When full, consider lots a little further away or those attached to commercial buildings and underground arcades.
Bicycles and motorbikes should use nearby bicycle/motorbike parking; riding into the park is not allowed.
parking.stationNote: Nearest station: about a 5-minute walk from Exit 5 of Fushimi Station (Higashiyama & Tsurumai subway lines).

officialManagement.title: About the Park
officialManagement.text: Shirakawa Park is a metropolitan park managed under the City of Nagoya's parks system, located in Naka Ward at the heart of the Sakae district. Together with the Nagoya City Science Museum and the Nagoya City Art Museum, which sit within its grounds, it forms a major cultural and green space for the city. Maintained as a public, free-access park, it serves residents and visitors alike as a place for relaxation, seasonal flower viewing and community events.

sections.title: Origins (1931)
sections.content: Shirakawa Park opened in 1931 (Showa 6), during a period when Nagoya was modernising its urban centre. It was laid out as a Western-style public park of open lawns and tree-lined promenades, reflecting the city's ambition to create green, recreational spaces for its citizens. The park takes its name from the Shirakawa (White River), a small stream that once flowed through this part of Nagoya before being culverted underground as the city expanded.

sections.title: Why Here?
sections.content: The site was chosen in the Sakae district because it sat between the city's growing cultural institutions and its commercial heart. Over time the park became the green front garden of two landmark museums: the Nagoya City Science Museum to the north and the Nagoya City Art Museum to the south. Its central, flat location made it an ideal gathering place and a calm counterpoint to the busy Sakae shopping district nearby.

sections.title: Cherry Blossoms & the Seasons
sections.content: Today the park is best known for its roughly 120 cherry trees, which draw crowds for hanami (blossom viewing) each spring. Beyond cherry season, the lawns, ginkgo avenues and water features make it a year-round retreat. The open, level grounds also host community events and markets, keeping the park woven into the daily life of Nagoya.

sections.title: A Green Heart of Nagoya
sections.content: Shirakawa Park remains one of central Nagoya's most accessible green spaces, free and open around the clock. Together with the museums on its grounds it forms a compact cultural quarter — a place where science, art and nature meet just steps from the Sakae skyline.

sections.title: A 'Green Lung' Reborn After the War
sections.content: Shirakawa Park suffered heavy air-raid damage during World War II. In the post-war years it was designated one of the two core green spaces of Nagoya's war-damage reconstruction plan (the other being Hisaya-odori Park). More than a place to relax, it became a green symbol of the city's rebirth from the ruins — entrusted with regulating the urban microclimate and healing citizens' spirits.

sections.title: The Vanished Shirakawa & Its Underground Culvert
sections.content: The park takes its name from the Shirakawa (White River) that once flowed here. To make room for the modern city, the stream was converted into a complex underground culvert. As you stroll the lawns, the clear water of old still flows quietly beneath your feet — a wonderful urban-geography teaching point.

sections.title: The World's Largest Planetarium
sections.content: Floating on the park's north side is the giant sphere of the Nagoya City Science Museum — the 'Brother Earth' planetarium. With a 35-metre inner diameter, it is certified by Guinness World Records as the 'world's largest planetarium', its shell of titanium panels radiating a futuristic, sci-fi feel.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: The giant metal sphere suspended between the museum buildings is Guinness-certified as the 'world's largest planetarium' (35 m inner diameter). Without leaving the park, you can frame a photo with a world-class scientific landmark.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Practical information on facilities, the park's history and planning your visit to Shirakawa Park.

items.q: Is there parking nearby? How much does it cost?
items.a: Shirakawa Park itself has no dedicated parking lot. Several paid municipal and private parking lots are within a 3–5 minute walk, mainly around the Sakae and Fushimi districts. Rates are typically charged by the hour; early arrival on weekends and during cherry season is recommended as they fill quickly.

items.q: How do I get to Shirakawa Park from Nagoya Station?
items.a: From Nagoya Station take the Higashiyama subway line about 3 minutes (one stop) to Fushimi Station, then walk about 5 minutes from Exit 5. You can also arrive via the Sakuradori line (Fushimi Station) or the Meijo line (Sakae Station). A taxi takes roughly 10 minutes.

items.q: Can wheelchairs or strollers get close?
items.a: Yes. The park is completely flat with paved, step-free paths, making it easy to navigate with wheelchairs, strollers and mobility aids. The adjacent museum entrances are also accessible.

items.q: Are there restrooms or food nearby?
items.a: Public restrooms are available within the park. For food and drinks, the surrounding Sakae district is full of cafés, restaurants and convenience stores a few minutes' walk away; the museums also have cafés.

items.q: When was the park founded and why is it special?
items.a: Shirakawa Park opened in 1931 as a Western-style public park, named after the Shirakawa river that once flowed nearby. It is special because it cradles two major museums — the Nagoya City Science Museum and the Nagoya City Art Museum — and is famous for about 120 cherry trees that turn the grounds pink each spring.

items.q: What is the Shirakawa river connection?
items.a: The park is named after the Shirakawa (White River), a small stream that originally ran through this area of Nagoya. As the city modernised, the river was culverted underground, but its name lives on in the park that became the neighbourhood's green heart.

items.q: Is it also written '白河公園'?
items.a: You may see it written as 白河公園, but the official name is 白川公園 (Shirakawa Park). 川 and 河 share the same reading, so they are easily confused — both refer to the same park in Sakae, Nagoya.
No. Shirakawa Park is a public park with free, 24-hour access — no ticket office or gate. (The museums on the grounds charge separate admission.)

items.q: How long does a visit take?
items.a: A relaxed visit lasts about 30 minutes to an hour: a stroll around the lawns, photos of the cherry blossoms or autumn leaves, and perhaps a rest on a bench. Allow extra time if you also enter the Science Museum or Art Museum.

items.q: Can I go in bad weather?
items.a: Yes — the park is open 24 hours and is outdoor, so it can be visited in any weather. In summer the sun is strong and shade is limited, so bring water and sun protection; after rain the paths may be damp but remain walkable.

items.q: After visiting, what else do you recommend nearby?
items.a: Right beside the park are the Nagoya City Science Museum (north) and the Nagoya City Art Museum (south). A short walk reaches Sakae's shopping and nightlife, Nagoya TV Tower and Hisaya-odori Park, while Nagoya Castle and the Osu shopping arcade are a little further by subway.

scienceArt.title: The Park's Core Institutions: Where Science Meets Art
scienceArt.subtitle: Shirakawa Park is more than greenery — it is a cultural and intellectual hub of Nagoya. Two internationally renowned museums sit on its flanks, blending with the natural setting.

scienceMuseum.name: Nagoya City Science Museum
scienceMuseum.role: Comprehensive modern science centre & interactive education
scienceMuseum.highlight: The giant sphere suspended between its buildings — the 'Brother Earth' planetarium — has a 35 m inner diameter and is Guinness-certified as the 'world's largest planetarium'; its titanium-panel shell radiates a futuristic, sci-fi feel.
points: Four core zones — Life Sciences, Science & Engineering and the Astronomical Theatre — covering science from the microscopic cell to the macroscopic universe.
Four signature experiences: an earthquake simulator reproducing magnitude 9, a 9 m 'Tornado Lab', a -30°C 'Deep Freeze Lab', and an 11 m high electrical-discharge stage.
Immersive demonstrations turn dry formulae into vivid visual spectacle.

artMuseum.name: Nagoya City Art Museum
artMuseum.highlight: The building was designed by Kisho Kurokawa, a grand master of Japanese contemporary architecture and a leading figure of the Metabolist movement, blending Western geometric aesthetics with traditional Edo imagery.
points: Four pillars of the permanent collection: local 'folk art' represented by Minori Kitagawa, the early-20th-century 'Mexican Renaissance', influential 'Surrealism', and 'contemporary cutting-edge art'.
A sunken courtyard flows naturally into the park's green slopes, breaking the museum's enclosed feel and letting art step into public leisure.
Modernist sculptures placed on the lawns turn the park into a 'museum without walls'.

outdoorMuseum.title: An Open-Air Science Micro-Museum: The Park's 'Hardcore' Landmarks
outdoorMuseum.subtitle: Walking the lawns and tree-lined paths, you'll find giant machines and sculptures — national treasures of Japan's industry, space, polar and marine exploration.

items.name: H-II Rocket Full-Scale Model
items.location: Outdoor plaza north of the Science Museum
items.background: A 1:1 replica of Japan's H-II large launch vehicle (nearly 50 m tall). The H-II, developed in the 1990s, was Japan's core liquid-fuel rocket and marked its full mastery of independent launch capability.
points: Examine up close the airframe, the huge first-stage engine nozzle and the solid rocket boosters (SRB) on either side.
Its soaring presence illustrates the principles of multi-stage propulsion and the sheer scale of space engineering.

items.name: Antarctic Overwintering Vehicle
items.background: This orange tracked vehicle is the actual 'SM50S' Antarctic overwintering vehicle used by the Japanese Antarctic Research Expedition (JARE) on the polar plateau in extreme cold, low pressure and blizzards.
points: Built with low-temperature steel, wide tracks and a heavily insulated cabin to operate at -60°C.
It carried scientists across hundreds of kilometres of uninhabited ice — hard evidence of humanity studying the planet's limits and global climate.

items.name: Historic Rail Relics (Train Sculptures)
items.location: Tree-lined path on the park's east side
items.background: The park preserves and displays classic trains marking Nagoya's industrial beginnings: a B6 steam locomotive and a retired Nagoya City Tram Type 1400.
points: B6 steam locomotive: a main freight engine imported from Britain in the Meiji era and later built domestically, showing the linkage aesthetics of early steam (external-combustion) power.
Type 1400 tram: the backbone of pre-war Nagoya's public transit, a living textbook on modern urban planning and electrified transport.

items.name: Marine-Research Machine Sculptures
items.location: Around the central fountain & water features
items.background: A sculpture group distilled or adapted from retired core components (metal propellers, anchor chains, deep-sea robot arms) of large deep-sea vessels and research ships such as the 'Chikyu' and 'Shinkai 6500'.
points: Their sharp streamlined hydrodynamic forms teach fluid dynamics and modern shipbuilding.
The cold machinery set against the lively fountain water creates a unique industrial landscape.

education.title: Why Talk About Science & Art in a Park? (The Meaning of Public Science)
education.subtitle: Shirakawa Park is no ordinary green space — it is Nagoya's ultimate laboratory for 'urban revival' and 'public education'.

points.title: Breaking the academic wall: 'effortless' science
points.text: Museums often feel exclusive, yet Shirakawa Park places national engineering relics like the H-II rocket and Antarctic vehicle right out on the lawns. Children touch rocket shells as they run; citizens gaze at the world's largest planetarium on a stroll — knowledge leaves the textbook and enters daily life.

points.title: Reshaping city memory: industry & technology in footprints
points.text: From a Meiji steam locomotive to a late-20th-century launch vehicle, from the vanished Shirakawa culvert to Kurokawa's Metabolism architecture, every exhibit is a coordinate of an era — showcasing Nagoya's modern story as Japan's 'manufacturing capital' (Monozukuri).

points.title: Inspiring cross-disciplinary thinking: science left, art right
points.text: The Science Museum to the north stands for reason, exploration and the future; the Art Museum to the south for feeling, reflection and humanity. Shirakawa Park is the ecological buffer between them, seeding a cross-disciplinary idea — that science ends in art, and art begins in science.

audience.title: Who Finds Their Resonance Here? (A Guide for Every Visitor)
audience.subtitle: Every visitor can find the way in that suits them best.

items.resonance: Immersive outdoor 'big toys' they can see and even touch, sparking curiosity about space and nature.
items.tip: Start on the lawn with the H-II rocket and Antarctic vehicle, then go inside the Science Museum for the 'Tornado' and 'Deep Freeze' labs.

items.resonance: Genuine hardcore machinery — a time-spanning dialogue between cutting-edge spacecraft and old steam locomotives.
items.tip: Focus on the H-II's LE-7 engine nozzle and the B6 locomotive's linkage aesthetics; allow plenty of time for close-up photos.

items.resonance: The geometric tension of Kurokawa's Metabolism architecture, the sci-fi floating sphere, and modernist sculptures scattered on the lawn.
items.tip: From 3 p.m. to dusk is best: sunlight through the trees hits the sunken courtyard and titanium sphere with striking lines.

items.resonance: Exploring the vanished Shirakawa culvert and Nagoya's post-war reconstruction planning.
items.tip: Avoid weekends; on a weekday morning walk the central axis south to north to read the spatial shift from classic Western garden to modern cultural quarter.

history.title: History & Significance of Shirakawa Park
history.subtitle: From a burnt-out district to the "Forest of Art and Science" — how this park grew in the heart of Nagoya.
paragraphs: Shirakawa Park is an urban park of roughly 8.9 hectares in Sakae 2-chome, Naka Ward, Nagoya. It holds two cultural institutions on its grounds — the Nagoya City Science Museum and the Nagoya City Art Museum — and in 2013 was given the nickname "Forest of Art and Science".

Its story is essentially a chapter of modern Nagoya. In 1942, as part of the celebrations for the 2,600th anniversary of the legendary founding of Japan, a park was planned for this district and, as the war deepened, designated an "air-defence park". On 12 March 1945 the Nagoya air raid reduced the Shirakawa district to ashes.

After the war the land was requisitioned and became "Castle Heights", a housing area for occupation forces' families. Returned in 1958, it was redeveloped by the city as a park and opened in 1967 to a design by the landscape architect Kimio Kondo.

timeline.title: Park plan begins
timeline.text: Planned as part of the 2,600th anniversary project and designated an air-defence park in wartime.

timeline.title: The Nagoya air raid
timeline.text: The raid of 12 March leaves the Shirakawa district burnt out.

timeline.title: Castle Heights
timeline.text: The land is requisitioned and becomes housing for occupation forces' families.

timeline.title: Return and redevelopment
timeline.text: The site is returned and work begins to create an urban park.

timeline.title: Science museum opens
timeline.text: The municipal Nagoya Science Museum, with astronomy and science buildings, opens.

timeline.title: Shirakawa Park opens
timeline.text: The park opens as an urban park to a design by the landscape architect Kimio Kondo.

timeline.title: Art museum opens
timeline.text: The Nagoya City Art Museum, designed by architect Kisho Kurokawa, opens on the south side.

timeline.title: Life Science building added
timeline.text: The museum is renamed Nagoya City Science Museum and its life science building opens.

timeline.title: Fountain unveiled
timeline.text: The fountain "Niji no Mai Shirakawa" is donated to mark a local broadcaster's 40th anniversary.

timeline.title: Sculpture Promenade
timeline.text: The Shirakawa Park Sculpture Promenade is developed, placing artworks throughout the grounds.

timeline.title: World's largest planetarium
timeline.text: The science museum's new planetarium, 35 m in diameter, opens and is certified by Guinness World Records.

timeline.title: A new nickname
timeline.text: The park is officially nicknamed the "Forest of Art and Science".

stories.title: Where the name "Shirakawa" comes from
stories.text: The park takes its name from Shirakawa-cho, the old district name. A waterway is said to have once run through the area, and its name survives in the place name — the park thus keeps alive the memory of a stream that has vanished.

stories.title: Recovery that began in ashes
stories.text: Immediately after the war, Shirakawa-cho was a burnt plain. That this land ended up preserved as a single large park site is the foundation of the greenery you see today.

stories.title: From military housing to a civic square
stories.text: During the occupation it was "Castle Heights", housing for American forces' families. Its conversion into lawns and tree-lined paths after the land was returned is a story emblematic of Nagoya's post-war recovery.

stories.title: An open-air gallery
stories.text: The Sculpture Promenade, developed from 1995, scattered sculptures across the grounds. The park became an "open exhibition room" where art appears mid-walk, not only inside the museum.

stories.title: A green corridor born of city planning
stories.text: Post-war reconstruction plans included 100-metre-wide boulevards, creating Wakamiya-odori and Hisaya-odori. Shirakawa Park sits beside this green axis and acts as a buffer within the built-up city.

stories.title: A fountain the city took to heart
stories.text: The fountain named "Niji no Mai Shirakawa" was donated by a local broadcaster for its 40th anniversary. Its sound and coolness make it a resting point on summer walks.

facts: The park covers about 8.9 hectares (89,300 m²), a large urban park next to the commercial district around Nagoya Station.
Having both the Nagoya City Science Museum and the Nagoya City Art Museum within a single park is unusual even by national standards.
The science museum's planetarium, "Brother Earth", is 35 m in diameter and was certified by Guinness World Records as the world's largest when it opened.
The name "Shirakawa" comes from the former district name and still survives in nearby intersection and bus stop names.
In cherry blossom season the park fills with local workers and families, and its benches and shade make ideal resting spots.
